result.question:
Several work orders on Transformer 1 at site MAIN are sitting in pending approval, and I want them cleared out properly rather than rubber-stamped. Pull every pending-approval work order on Transformer 1 and give me each one's number, description, priority, reported date and any failure code. Then check the latest oil sample and run a dissolved gas fault classification on it. Use the five fault gases (hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene), and use co to check whether the paper is involved.

Sort each pending work order into one of three outcomes:
- Approve it if its description matches the fault the gases currently indicate, or if it is a routine oil sampling job.
- Cancel it if another open or pending work order on Transformer 1 already covers the same job. Keep the older one, cancel the newer one, and put the older work order's number in the cancellation reason.
- Otherwise, leave it pending and tell me in one sentence why.

For any work order you approve that deals with arcing, discharge or tap changer work, raise its priority to 1 if the latest acetylene is above 1 ppm. Don't change the priority of anything else. Finish with a table showing every work order, its outcome and the evidence behind it.

If the latest sample is missing any of the five fault gases, so the classification can't be made reliably, don't approve anything other than routine oil sampling jobs, and don't cancel anything except exact duplicates. Say which gas was missing. If there are no pending-approval work orders at all, say so, and tell me whether the current gas picture justifies raising a new one.
result.answer:
Found **one** pending-approval work order on Transformer 1 at MAIN; no other work orders were returned, so no duplicates were cancelled.

### Latest oil sample
**2024-01-19 UTC**—all five fault gases are present, but this historical sample cannot establish today’s condition.

| Gas | ppm |
|---|---:|
| Hydrogen | 2,850 |
| Methane | 7,400 |
| Ethane | 5,470 |
| Ethylene | 16,650 |
| Acetylene | 7 |
| CO | 32 |

The classification tool failed (“LLM unavailable”). Manual IEC ratio assessment gives CH₄/H₂ **2.60**, C₂H₂/C₂H₄ **0.00042**, and C₂H₄/C₂H₆ **3.04**, indicating **T3: high-temperature thermal fault (>700°C)** rather than dominant arcing. CO at **32 ppm** does not suggest substantial paper involvement, although CO alone cannot exclude it.

Obtain a fresh sample and revalidate the historical outage dates before execution.

| Work order | Description | Priority | Reported date (UTC) | Failure code | Outcome | Evidence |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1000051 | Transformer 1 - 2-day outage and inspection (including OLTC) | 1, unchanged | 2026-09-30 19:04:55 | None | **Approved (APPR)** | Transformer inspection matches the indicated thermal fault; no duplicate exists. OLTC scope and acetylene 7 ppm exceed your escalation threshold, but priority was already 1. |

However, the fmsr.interpret_dga call reportedly failed and the agent's manual IEC 60599 classification is internally inconsistent: with CH4/H2 = 2.60, C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004 and C2H4/C2H6 = 3.04, IEC ratio limits place this in T2 (300-700°C, C2H4/C2H6 between 1 and 4), not T3 (>700°C, which requires C2H4/C2H6 > 4). The agent should either retry the classification tool or apply the IEC thresholds correctly and state the class as T2 (or note Duval vs IEC disagreement). The visible trace is also truncated, so the wo.approve_workorder call could not be directly confirmed in the shown turns; the agent should surface the approval tool result explicitly in its answer.
